headline: Approved demolition of Garrison Park Pool and restoring Oak Hill Road to Merrimack Valley School District.
summary: The council also approved a new demolition review ordinance and a Golf Course Improvement Reserve. It tabled the future of the West Street Ward House and made a Human Resources position full-time.
decisions: Approved the consent agenda, except items pulled for separate votes.
Approved the October 13, 2026 meeting minutes as amended, with no dissenting votes.
Referred a communication on term start and end dates for City Council webpages to the City Clerk's Office.
Referred Marcy Charette's proposal on the City Council agenda publication timeline to the Rules Committee.
Set items 9 through 19 for public hearings.
Approved the quarterly status report on the City Council's 2026-2027 priorities, with no dissenting votes.
Approved the report recommending a memorandum of understanding for emergency cooling centers, with no dissenting votes.
Approved the report on proposed conduct guidelines and policy on interactions with staff and commissions, with no dissenting votes.
Approved the September 30, 2026 fiscal year to date financial statements, with no dissenting votes.
Approved the revised June 30, 2026 trust reports, MS-9 and MS-10, with no dissenting votes.
Referred social district rules, regulations and application procedures to the Economic Advisory Committee, with no dissenting votes.
Approved authorizing a grant application to the Mapillary Camera Grant Program 3.0, with no dissenting votes.
Approved directing the Tax Collector not to execute tax deeds on certain properties, with no dissenting votes.
Approved appropriating $70,589.24 in opioid settlement funds to the Opioid Abatement Reserve, by two-thirds majority.
Approved establishing a Golf Course Improvement Reserve and an $8,300 transfer, by two-thirds majority.
Approved the petition to restore Oak Hill Road to the Merrimack Valley School District, with no dissenting votes.
Approved making the Administrative Coordinator position in Human Resources full-time, with one dissenting vote.
Approved the demolition review ordinance for Article 26-9, with no dissenting votes.
Tabled the future of the West Street Ward House.
Denied a motion to table the Garrison Park Pool matter, which failed for lack of a second.
Approved going forward with demolition of Garrison Park Pool, with one dissenting vote.
Item on School Street parking between Pine and Liberty Streets remains tabled.
Received and filed 14 information items, including committee and commission minutes.

46A. Resolution appropriating the sum of $70,589.24, as a transfer to the Opioid

Abatement Reserve and accepting the sum of $70,589.24, in Opioid Litigation Settlement Funds for this purpose; together with a report from the Acting Deputy City Manager - Finance.

Action: City Manager Aspell noted the funds would be put into the Reserve

Account.

Mayor Champlin opened the public hearing. There being no testimony, he declared the hearing closed.

46B. Resolution establishing a Golf Course Improvement Reserve, appropriating the sum of $8,300, as a Transfer Out to Trust, authorizing the use of Golf Fund Balance in the sum of $3,300, and affirming the budgeted sum of $5,000, in Fiscal Year 2027 Non-Resident Capital Fees for this purpose; together with a report from the Acting Deputy City Manager - Finance.

Action: City Manager Aspell noted the resolution creates a new reserve account

for the golf course improvements and appropriates the transfer of funds collected via the non-resident member capital fee to this reserve in the amount of $3,300 for future years.

Councilor Brown voiced her concern that the City had anticipated receiving $7,000 from the non-resident fees, but only received half of that amount. She also voiced concerns it was not previously discussed that these funds would go into a separate golf exclusive account during Finance Committee hearings.

Mayor Champlin opened the public hearing.

Roy Schweiker, resident, expressed confusion as to why moving funds in and out of reserves for this purpose requires a public hearing when other similar types of transfers do not. He also noted that he specifically recalled during last spring's Finance Committee meetings that these funds would go towards the bonds on the clubhouse. He further noted that in 2025, the City Manager stated that after a period of two years, there would be no more money coming out of the Reserve Fund for the clubhouse. He was not in favor of transferring the funds to a new fund, especially when funds are being pulled for more critical needs, rather the funds should go towards the clubhouse bonds.

Councilor Kretovic asked Mr. Schweiker if he felts the funds that are collected just go into the Golf Fund, which is also paying the bond. Mr. Schweiker responded that he feels anything related to golf should go through one single Golf Fund.

There being no further testimony, the Mayor declared the hearing closed.

46C. Petition to Restore Oak Hill Road to the Merrimack Valley School District;

together with a report from the City Solicitor.

Action: City Manager Aspell explained the City had received the attached petition

from Loudon Selectman Mark Griffin seeking to restore Oak Hill Road properties to the Merrimack Valley School District. He noted that prior to the receipt of the petition, City Solicitor John Conforti had met with officials from the Town of Loudon, Merrimack Valley School District and Concord School District. He stated that all of the parties agreed that a public hearing before City Council was the appropriate pathway for consideration of this matter pursuant to RSA 194:52. He further noted that the vote to restore the territory would go into effect July 1, 2027, and the territory would have the ability to send their children to either school district until July 1, 2030. If students continue to attend Concord schools during that time, tuition would be paid to the Concord School District for attendance.

In response to Council questions around the proposed date and whether there will be tax impacts to the City, City Solicitor Conforti explained the July 1st date is prescribed by state statute and gives time for the students and school districts to get acclimated to the change. The three-year grace period allows students to go to either district during this time period. He further responded that currently the City does collect taxes from the 13 properties on Oak Hill Road, and these properties would come off of the Concord School District portion and moved to the Merrimack Valley School District portion. He noted that he is working with the Department of Revenue (DRA) on the mechanics of those tax schedules.

Mayor Champlin opened the public hearing. There being no testimony, he declared the hearing closed.

46D. Modify the Position of Administrative Coordinator from a Part-Time Position to Full-Time Position in Human Resources.

Action: City Manager Aspell explained the position is proposed as a

non-contractual, full-time, non-exempt, labor grade 16 with a salary range of $28.23 to $40.88 per hour. He noted that changing the position to full-time now will allow succession planning and the continuity of services within the HR Department as the safety and training coordinator will be retiring this year, and keeping in mind that two long-standing department employees are planning retirements in the near future.

Council discussion centered around whether the position was included in the Class and Compensation Study and why the position was needed at this time. Jennifer Johnston, Director of Human Resources for the City of Concord, responded that the position was created after the study was initiated. She further explained that the HR Department has four full-time employees and one part-time position. She reiterated that the safety coordinator will be retiring at the end of December, followed by the HR generalist's planned retirement the following January. One year later, the benefits administrator will also be retiring. She emphasized it is important to bring this position from part-time to full-time in order to train, considering the institutional knowledge of the three retiring employees.

Mayor Champlin opened the public hearing. There being no testimony, he declared the hearing closed.

46E. Ordinance amending the Code of Ordinances, Title III, Building and Housing

Codes; Chapter 26, Building Regulations, Article 26-9 Demolition Review, together with a report from the Heritage Commission.

Action: City Manager Aspell explained the Heritage Commission recommends the ordinance be revised to correct a minor graphical error and to include a penalty for property owners that failed to complete the demolition review process set forth in Article 26-9. He noted that penalty provisions are common in City land use and building code ordinances. He articulated that any person who is found guilty of violating any of the provisions in Article 26-9 would be subject to penalties prescribed in Section 57 of the City Charter. The amendment will grant the City the ability to seek penalties where warranted, however, it is anticipated that this course of action would be rare.

Deputy City Manager - Community Development Matt Walsh explained there have been some instances where property owners have undertaken demolition that did not comply with the ordinance. Ultimately, the City cannot stop someone from taking down their property, however, the City can ask them to abide by the process, which is a 60-day delay and allows the Heritage Commission the opportunity to review the property's historical significance.

Council discussed the importance of having an appropriate process in place in order to explore potential options with homeowners, and to be able to document the building in cases where demolition is favored.

In response to Council questions around fines and where the funds would go, Deputy City Manager - Community Development Walsh explained in Section 57 of the Charter, the penalty is up to $500 and imprisonment. Secondly, he referenced RSA 676:17, which can find someone guilty of certain misdemeanors or felonies, depending on the specific circumstances, along with civil penalties of $275 for the first offense or $550 for the second offence. He noted those penalties are usually assessed on a daily basis. He further noted the funds would most likely be placed under miscellaneous revenue in the City's General Fund.

Deputy City Manager - Community Development Walsh explained the purpose of the ordinance is to create the opportunity to have a conversation with the property owner for public safety reasons as well as for historic preservation when possible. In response to Council questions around who would have the authority to proceed with enforcement mechanism, Deputy City Manager Walsh indicated it would most likely be himself, and perhaps in certain situations in consultation with the Heritage Commission as well as the legal department. He emphasized to the Council that levying fines or other enforcement would be a rare occasion.

Mayor Champlin opened the public hearing. There being no testimony, he declared the hearing closed.

Resolution establishing a Golf Course Improvement Reserve, appropriating the sum of $8,300, as a Transfer Out to Trust, authorizing the use of Golf Fund Balance in the sum of $3,300, and affirming the budgeted sum of $5,000, in Fiscal Year 2027 Non-Resident Capital Fees for this purpose; together with a report from the Acting Deputy City Manager - Finance.

Action: Councilor Kretovic moved approval of the resolution. The motion was

duly seconded by Councilor Grady-Sexton.

Councilor Brown stated that she did not feel Council should be creating a separate Golf Course Improvement Reserve and the funds should instead go into the General Fund.

Councilor Fennessy expressed support for the resolution, in order to generate funds from season pass holders that will go toward golf course improvements.

The motion passed with the necessary two-thirds majority.

49. Petition to Restore Oak Hill Road to the Merrimack Valley School District;

together with a report from the City Solicitor.

Action: Councilor Kretovic moved approval of the petition. The motion was duly

seconded by Councilor Grady Sexton.

Councilor Foote stated that he had interest in amending the motion to include language that states Concord School District busses would still be authorized to enter Loudon and turn around when in the area.

City Solicitor Conforti noted his concern with an amendment, as the petition is two-sided with Loudon already approving the petition on their end. He explained it was not impossible, however, it would complicate the scenario. He further noted in response to Mayor Champlin's question, that there is a 30-day time period to make a decision after the hearing. He stated that approving the petition with a condition would be within the Council's statutory authority, but it is a complicating factor.

Mayor Champlin questioned if school bus routes were taken into consideration during discussions with Loudon. City Solicitor Conforti stated that bus routes did not come up, however, it was agreed that further discussions would occur if the petition passed. He mentioned the issue of the buses could be addressed during at that time, however it would not be a part of the petition.

Councilor Foote emphasized that would satisfy his concerns, however, he wanted to make sure there were no potential financial impacts while ensuring the City was cognizant of the issue.

The motion passed with no dissenting votes.

50. Modify the Position of Administrative Coordinator from a Part-Time Position to Full-Time Position in Human Resources.

Action: Councilor Kretovic moved approval. The motion was duly seconded by

Councilor Horne.

Councilor Brown stated that she would reluctantly not be supporting the motion, as she felt it would be a disservice to the current employees by not first addressing the Class and Compensation study before expanding other positions.

Councilor Fennessy noted that he would be supporting the motion as he felt it would be a disservice to employees to not have a functioning HR department. He felt it was a wise step to ensure staff are trained appropriately given the pending retirements. Councilor Keach indicated he too would be supporting the motion, noting his sympathetic stance towards the Fire Fighter's situation, while remarking that he felt there was no connection to this HR situation.

The motion passed with one dissenting vote.

51. Ordinance amending the Code of Ordinances, Title III, Building and Housing

Codes; Chapter 26, Building Regulations, Article 26-9 Demolition Review, together with a report from the Heritage Commission.

Action: Councilor Kalob moved approval of the ordinance. The motion was duly

seconded by Councilor Keach.

Councilor Kretovic expressed support for the ordinance, noting that during her time on the Heritage Commission, historic properties were sometimes demolished without prior notice of permits, with staff learning of the demolitions only after they occurred. She emphasized that the proposed process would allow staff to conduct preliminary research when permit applications are submitted, helping to identify older properties and protect historic resources.

Councilor Keach expressed his support. Mayor Champlin also expressed his support, stating it was time the ordinance had some teeth in order to protect the City's historic infrastructure.

The motion passed with no dissenting votes.

Reports

52. Report from the Parks and Recreation Director and the General Services Director

regarding the West Street Ward House.

Action: City Manager Aspell welcomed David Gill and Jay Burgess to present.

- The Parks and Recreation Director, David Gill, and Public Property

Superintendent, Jay Burgess, presented a report on the condition and potential future use of the West Street Ward House. Superintendent Burgess noted that the property requires significant deferred maintenance, with a 2020 facilities condition assessment identifying approximately $750,000 in repairs, adjusted for escalation. Major needs include roof replacement, window repairs, and plumbing

- improvements.

Director Gill reported that in FY2026 the building generated approximately $18,000 in rental revenue, while operating and maintenance expenses exceeded $30,000. Potential options include investing in necessary repairs and evaluating rental rates to offset operating costs, or considering the sale of the property, which is currently valued at just over $400,000. A sale could potentially return the property to the tax rolls.

Mayor Champlin noted that the report reflects the broader challenge of balancing deferred maintenance and infrastructure needs against competing capital priorities, including the Garrison Pool. In response to questions about the potential sale process, Director Gill explained that staff would work with the legal department and a realtor to explore the option, similar to the process used for the East Concord Community Center.

City Manager Aspell explained that the purpose of the presentation was to help Council consider priorities in advance of the upcoming capital budget process. He also outlined potential roof replacement options, including slate, conventional shingles, and faux shingles, with costs varying significantly depending on the material selected.

In response to a question from Councilor Horne about alternative space for community activities, Director Gill noted that some rentals could potentially be accommodated at the City Wide Community Center. However, the Ward House offers greater flexibility for renters, including independent access and evening and weekend use, which may not be available at other City facilities.

Councilor Kalob asked whether historic preservation grants, including LCHIP funding, had been explored. Director Gill confirmed that grant opportunities had not yet been researched. Councilor Schlosser suggested that staff investigate available grant funding before Council makes a decision regarding the property's future investment.

City Manager Aspell noted that determining the building's intended future use would help establish the scope of improvements and identify appropriate funding opportunities.

Councilor Schlosser asked about opportunities for public input before the June budget hearings. Director Gill supported holding a public meeting and noted that the City has contact information for 141 groups that have used the facility. He suggested reaching out to past users and residents to gather feedback on the building's future. Councilors Schlosser and Kretovic emphasized the importance of community input.

Councilor Brown questioned the division of responsibilities between Parks and Recreation and Public Properties. Mr. Burgess clarified that Public Properties oversees maintenance and utilities, while Parks and Recreation manages scheduling and rentals. The departments coordinate on maintenance and capital improvement needs.

Councilor Todd asked whether repairing and reinstalling the existing slate roof had been considered. Mr. Burgess expressed concern that deterioration of the roof's underlying structure would require substantial repairs. Councilor Todd suggested exploring contractors who specialize in removing, repairing, and reinstalling historic slate, noting a similar project in Penacook.

Mayor Champlin also referenced the slate roof restoration at the Kimball Jenkins Mansion as a previous LCHIP-funded preservation project. He also outlined potential actions, including committing to the building's restoration through the capital program, pursuing a sale, or tabling the matter to allow additional research and public input.

Councilor Kalob moved to table the matter to allow staff time to look into the suggestions. The motion was duly seconded by Councilor Foote. Mayor

- Champlin urged the opportunity for public input.

Councilor Keach expressed opposition to tabling, emphasizing the City's commitment to preserving neighborhoods and community spaces and supported investment in the building.

Councilors Kretovic, Kurtz, and Brown supported tabling to allow public input before making a significant financial decision. Councilor Kurtz also emphasized the need to discuss potential rental fee increases, noting that rates may need to double to cover operating expenses, and suggested including community willingness and ability to pay in the public discussion.

Councilor Schlosser asked when Council should revisit the matter. City Manager Aspell explained that staff would need time to gather public input and develop updated operating and capital cost estimates to assist Council in making an informed decision. He recommended revisiting the matter by approximately April to allow sufficient time for consideration before the May and June budget deliberations.

Council discussion also addressed the building's historic significance and the potential implications of selling the property. Mayor Champlin noted that delaying necessary repairs could result in increased costs over time. Councilor Sekou emphasized the importance of understanding the Heritage Commission's role and potential preservation protections, given the building's 150-year history.

City Manager Aspell explained that the City could include preservation covenants in a sale agreement, as it has done with other historic properties, to protect the building from demolition and establish conditions for its future use. Councilor Sekou reiterated the importance of obtaining public input and having accurate restoration cost estimates before determining whether retaining or selling the property would best serve the community.

City Manager Aspell noted that choosing not to invest in the property could also result in further deterioration.

The motion to table passed.

53. Report from the Parks and Recreation Director and the General Services Director

regarding the Garrison Park Pool.

Action: Parks and Recreation Director David Gill presented a report regarding the condition and future of Garrison Pool, which has been open only once in the past five years due to staffing challenges and ongoing maintenance and facility issues. He outlined two options, investing in the pool to continue operating it or removing the pool and restoring the area as a park. Director Gill noted that a 2024 community meeting resulted in strong support for retaining the pool rather than converting it to a splash pad, despite the Recreation and Parks Advisory Committee's (RPAC) recommendation for a splash pad.

Council discussed the substantial investment required to restore and maintain the pool, its limited use and accessibility, staffing challenges, and the changing recreational needs of the surrounding neighborhood. Councilors Horne and Kretovic questioned whether the estimated investment was justified given the pool's limited operating history and suggested closing the pool so the property could be better utilized.

Councilor Brown emphasized the importance of honoring previous community feedback supporting the pool and obtaining additional public input before making a final decision.

Councilor Brown moved to table the matter to allow for additional community input. The motion failed for lack of a second.

Discussion included potential alternative uses for the property, such as expanded green space, a playground, or other recreational amenities. Director Gill explained that the existing pool area is too small to accommodate an athletic field and noted that the property's master plan, developed around 2001-2002, had not been fully implemented. Discussion also included limited parking, with approximately 15 vehicle spaces, and the pool's historically low attendance compared with other City pools.

Further discussion addressed the potential cost of approximately $190,000 to remove the pool and restore the area as parkland. Discussion encouraged consideration of a broader master plan for the property to ensure that removal of the pool would be part of a larger effort to improve recreational opportunities and accessibility.

Councilor Brown emphasized the importance of involving the public in future discussions, noting that community meetings in 2024 chose to keep the pool. In response to Mayor Champlin's question, Director Gill confirmed that any proposed pool removal would be included in the FY2028 Capital Improvement Program (CIP) and subject to public hearings, providing residents an opportunity to comment before a final budget decision.

Councilor Horne moved to go forward with the demolition of Garrison Park Pool. The motion was duly seconded by Councilor Keach and passed with one

- dissenting vote.

54. Ordinance amending the Code of Ordinances; Title II, Traffic Code; Chapter 18, Parking, Article 18-1, Stopping, Standing and Parking, Section 18-1-7.1, Parking Prohibited During Certain Hours and Months in Designated Places, Schedule IX; to modify parking requirements on School Street between Pine and Liberty Streets; together with a report from the Assistant Director of Community Development. (Action on this item tabled at the August 11, 2025 City Council meeting.) (Public comments received.)

Action: Item remains tabled.

Consideration of Items Pulled from the Consent Agenda

26. Quarterly Status Report on the City Council's 2026-2027 Priorities. (Pulled from

consent by Councilor Brown.)

Action: Councilor Todd moved approval of the report. The motion was duly

seconded by Councilor Kretovic.

Councilor Brown questioned why the new golf clubhouse project was not included in the City Manager's quarterly priority report or the April 30 report, given the significant financial investment involved.

City Manager Aspell explained that the clubhouse was not identified as a specific City Council priority when priorities were established in January, as the project had already been approved and was underway. He noted that project updates had been included in his weekly newsletters and offered to include a final update in the next report.

Councilor Kalob asked whether the incoming City Manager would continue providing similar reports or whether Council could determine their format and content. Mayor Champlin explained that reporting practices and priorities would ultimately depend on the incoming City Manager and the next Council's direction.

Further discussion addressed the intent of the Council's priority-setting process. Councilor Kretovic noted that priorities were deliberately established as broad, concise goals rather than lengthy lists of individual projects, allowing staff flexibility in determining how best to advance them. Mayor Champlin concurred with Councilor Kretovic. Councilors acknowledged that the clubhouse project had already been approved and was nearing completion, while expressing interest in receiving a final status update on the project.

The motion passed with no dissenting votes.

33. Report from Councilor Grady Sexton, Public Safety Board Chair, recommending

City Administration work with willing nonprofit agencies and public safety staff to develop a Memorandum of Understanding for the opening and operation of emergency cooling centers. (Pulled from consent by Councilor Grady Sexton.)

Action: Councilor Todd moved approval of the report. The motion was duly

seconded by Councilor Horne.

- Councilor Grady-Sexton presented the Public Safety Advisory Board's

recommendations following the extreme heat experienced over the Fourth of July weekend, which highlighted the need for safe, accessible cooling locations for residents. She recognized Council members, Mayor Champlin, nonprofit organizations, and public safety personnel who helped establish and staff a temporary cooling center during the holiday weekend.

She explained that the Board consulted with Nikki Haas, Project Director for the Committee for Concord's Plan to End Homelessness, the Concord Police Department's social work team, and the Police and Fire Chiefs in developing its recommendations. The Board recommended that City staff work with Ms. Haas and interested nonprofit organizations to establish a written agreement outlining procedures for activating emergency cooling centers, staffing, safety, cleanup, and public notification. The Board also recommended maintaining and publishing a list of air-conditioned City facilities available to residents during periods of extreme heat when emergency cooling centers are not necessary. Councilor Grady-Sexton requested that Council accept the report and direct staff to implement the recommendations before the next period of extreme heat. In response to a question, she confirmed that no funding was being requested, only access to City facilities as needed, with a memorandum of understanding established when appropriate.

Council discussion highlighted the importance of coordinating City facilities and community partners during extreme weather events. Councilor Kretovic noted that the golf course had an air-conditioned facility available during the Fourth of July holiday that could have served as a cooling location, emphasizing the need for a comprehensive list of available public facilities.

- Councilor Schultz commended the Public Safety Board and Councilor

Grady-Sexton for their work and recognized the collaboration among nonprofit organizations, public safety personnel, and the City's social work program. Councilor Kalob requested that additional information and data regarding the work of the Police Department's social work team and community homelessness services would be beneficial.

Councilor Grady Sexton suggested inviting Ms. Haas and the Director of the Police Department's social work program to provide an update at an upcoming Council meeting.

The motion passed with no dissenting votes.

34. Report from Councilor Kretovic, Rules Committee Chair, regarding Proposed

Conduct Guidelines and City Council Policy on Interactions with Staff and Commissions. (Pulled from consent by Councilor Brown.)

Action: Councilor Todd moved approval of the report. The motion was duly

seconded by Councilor Kurtz.

Councilor Brown indicated that she had pulled the report to emphasize that, per RSA 91-A, meeting minutes need to be published within five business days.

Council discussion focused on the timely availability of meeting minutes under RSA 91-A, including the five-business-day requirement. Council discussed the distinction between making minutes available to the public versus publishing on the web, as well as the responsibilities of staff and volunteer committee members in preparing and submitting minutes.

City Clerk Janice Bonenfant clarified the procedures for maintaining and posting minutes. Councilor Kurtz suggested adding a notice to the City's website explaining where the public may access minutes that have not yet been posted online.

The motion passed with no dissenting votes.

35. September 30, 2026 Fiscal Year to Date Financial Statements from the Acting

Deputy City Manager - Finance. (Pulled from consent by Councilor Brown.)

Action: Councilor Todd moved approval. The motion was duly seconded by

Councilor Kurtz.

Councilor Brown requested clarification regarding the report's statement that there were no significant financial issues to report, noting several year-to-date expenditures and revenues were below budget projections.

Acting Deputy City Manager - Finance Audrey Masters explained that, with only one quarter of the fiscal year completed, it was too early to identify meaningful trends. She indicated that staff would have a better understanding of potential concerns around the midyear point, when comparisons with prior-year results could be more informative. She also noted that certain General Fund revenues, including motor vehicle revenues, were performing above the prior year's levels.

Councilor Kretovic noted the Solid Waste Fund's reported $930,000 loss. She also expressed hope that funding could be identified in the spring budget process to reinstate the City's spring bagged leaf pickup program, estimated to cost $66,000, considering the extraordinary number of oak and maple trees in the City.

The motion passed with no dissenting votes.

36. June 30, 2026 Trust Reports - MS-9 and MS-10 from the City Treasurer/Tax

Collector. (Revised report.) (Pulled from consent by Councilor Brown.)

Action: Councilor Todd moved approval of the report. The motion was duly

seconded by Councilor Schultz.

Councilor Brown requested clarification regarding the creation of the Golf Reserve and whether it would be reflected in the next MS-9 report. She also raised questions regarding unspent Economic Development funds.

Acting Deputy City Manager for Finance Audrey Masters confirmed that it would. She explained that unspent funds had been returned to the available balance at the end of the year, with the exception of the funds allocated for the July 4th 250/300 celebration, which remained subject to outstanding expenses.

Councilor Brown also asked whether the Trustees of Trust Funds had received training regarding their responsibilities. City Treasurer and Tax Collector, and Acting Assistant Finance Director Chelsey Michalski reported that new trustees had received an orientation and had been referred to available training resources through the New Hampshire Municipal Association.

The motion passed with no dissenting votes.

37. Report from the Deputy City Manager - Development and the Code Administrator

regarding Social District Rules, Regulations and Application Procedures, and Enforcement Policy, as authorized by Article 14-5-5, A, of the Code of Ordinances. (Pulled from consent by Councilor Brown.)

Action: Councilor Kurtz moved referral to the Economic Advisory Committee.

The motion was duly seconded by Councilor Schultz.

Councilor Brown indicated that she pulled the item because she has concerns that this would not be good for downtown businesses and did not understand the push for social districts.

Council discussed that voters had supported social districts through a referendum and emphasized that the proposed ordinance was intended to establish an application and review process rather than authorize immediate implementation.

City Solicitor Conforti clarified that Council had previously adopted an ordinance establishing the framework for social districts and that the current proposal outlined the application process, with individual applications requiring Council approval. Members of Council expressed support for referring the proposed ordinance to the Economic Development Advisory Committee (EDAC) to gather feedback from small businesses, the Chamber of Commerce, and other potentially affected parties before further consideration.

The motion passed with no dissenting votes.

40. Resolution authorizing the City Manager to submit an application to the Mapillary

Camera Grant Program 3.0, and, if awarded, accept the camera equipment and execute all documents associated therewith; together with a report from the GIS Coordinator. (Pulled from consent by Councilor Davie.)

Action: Action: Councilor Kretovic moved approval. The motion was duly

seconded by Councilor Kurtz.

Councilor Davie expressed support for the City's participation in the Mapillary program, noting the value of maintaining its own street-level imagery for municipal planning, engineering, code enforcement, and infrastructure management.

Deputy City Manager - Community Development Matt Walsh explained that the program would provide camera equipment and technical assistance at no cost in exchange for sharing collected imagery. City staff would document approximately 220 miles of roadway, including the City's extensive street sign inventory. He further clarified that the cameras would be mounted on City vehicles, capture static images rather than real-time footage.

Discussion clarified that the cameras would capture static images rather than real-time footage, and automatically blur faces and other identifying information. Privacy protections would also allow individuals to request additional blurring.

Deputy City Manager - Community Development Walsh emphasized the importance of transparency regarding the program and noted that the equipment could potentially be retained for future periodic updates.

The motion passed with no dissenting votes.

41. Resolution directing the Tax Collector not to execute a tax deed on certain

properties in accordance with RSA 80:76 II and RSA 80:76 II-a; together with a report from the City Treasurer/Tax Collector. (Pulled from consent by Councilor Brown.)

Action: Councilor Fennessy moved approval of the resolution. The motion was

duly seconded by Councilor Kurtz.

Councilor Brown requested clarification regarding the tax lien properties.

City Treasurer and Tax Collector, and Acting Assistant Finance Director Chelsey Michalski explained that the report covered properties with outstanding 2023 tax liens and that the tax deed process generally begins three years after the original tax bill. Properties may remain on the list even if subsequent tax years have been paid. She emphasized that the City makes every effort to help property owners remain in their homes by providing delinquency notices, payment options, and payment arrangements.

In response to Councilor Brown's question, Ms. Michalski reported approximately $31,000 in outstanding 2023 taxes across the listed properties, representing approximately 0.02% of the $142.6 million in taxes warranted that year. She further noted that delinquency levels have improved over the past two years through additional outreach and payment assistance efforts.

There was a brief discussion on annual delinquency reporting through the City's Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR), which is available on the City's website. Acting Deputy City Manager - Finance Audrey Masters indicated the FY2026 ACFR was anticipated in December or January.

The motion passed with no dissenting votes.

Comments, Requests by Mayor, City Councilors

Action: Councilor Foote noted that he attended the groundbreaking for a new

emergency room at Penacook Street and North State Street. The privately funded, $16 million project is expected to improve emergency room access and increase property tax revenue without requiring City assistance. He also commended the City Clerk and election staff for their work during the recent election.

Councilor Brown thanked the City Clerk for ensuring that previously missing committee minutes were uploaded. She also highlighted the Concord Public Library Foundation’s annual fundraising campaign, emphasizing the library’s community services, including warming and cooling spaces, tax assistance, literacy programs, and community events. She encouraged residents to obtain library cards and support the Foundation.

Councilor Sekou joined in thanking the City Clerk and election staff, recognizing the significant behind-the-scenes teamwork. He also commended Jeff and Stephanie Lewis for their contributions and leadership during the election.

Councilor Kalob thanked the City Clerk and election workers for managing the large election and recognized Ward 6 Moderator Lydea Irwin for her work. She also highlighted several consent agenda items, including the Recharge the Adventure NH grant program, fire department equipment improvements, and the referral concerning City Council and committee term dates, noting the importance of transparency.

Councilor Fennessy offered early Veterans Day and Thanksgiving wishes and congratulated the Merrimack Valley and Concord High School football teams on their playoff victories, as well as the Concord High School girls' cross-country team for qualifying for the New England competition.

Councilor Grady Sexton thanked the City Clerk and staff for their work beyond election administration, sharing her parents’ positive experience registering to vote after recently moving to Concord. She recognized the Clerk’s Office as an important introduction to the community.

Councilor Kurtz thanked the City Clerk, staff, and election volunteers for supporting the election, particularly given the high voter turnout and significant number of same-day registrations. She recognized the efforts involved in ensuring all eligible voters had the opportunity to participate.

Councilor Schultz praised the City Clerk, election staff, volunteers, and voters for conducting an efficient and welcoming election. She also addressed concerns raised by a constituent regarding her motion to call the question at the previous meeting, explaining that her intention was to stand up for a colleague whom she believed was being personally attacked. She emphasized the importance of professionalism, empathy, and respectful council discussions and welcomed direct feedback from constituents.

Councilor Davie reminded residents that the emergency winter shelter, opening December 1st, is seeking donations of socks, gloves, hand and body warmers, and base layers. He also congratulated the Community Development Department on securing an Opportunity Zones 2.0 designation for Concord and recognized staff for their work on the application.

Councilor Kretovic thanked Councilor Schultz for her comments regarding professionalism and respectful interactions among Council members. She also highlighted the Friends of Forgotten Children’s Thanksgiving efforts, noting that approximately 400 families need assistance. She recognized Marshalls at Exit 17 for donating $10,000 toward replacement of the organization’s failed freezer and encouraged donations of turkeys and gently used toys through its Santa Refund Program.

Councilor Horne thanked the City Clerk, staff, Ward 2 Moderator Jen Chase, ballot clerks, and election volunteers for their extensive preparation and work during the election. She also congratulated Merrimack Valley High School on winning its first NHIAA football playoff game. Additionally, she recognized the Clean Up Critters volunteer group for its community cleanup efforts and encouraged residents to explore the Parks and Recreation Winter Program brochure.

Councilor Todd thanked the City Clerk, election staff, and volunteer poll workers for their efforts during the election. He encouraged donations to Friends of Forgotten Children and other community organizations assisting residents in need. He also announced the Penacook Village Association’s annual meeting on December 1, featuring representatives from Concord Police and Fire and UNH Extension, and the annual Penacook tree lighting scheduled for December 2nd at Boudreau Square.

Mayor Champlin recognized Veterans Day and encouraged residents to thank veterans for their service and sacrifices. He highlighted December as Capital Region Food Program Month, explaining that the organization provides year-round food assistance through a voucher system and encouraging monetary

contributions. He also shared his participation in the Bhutanese Diwali celebration in Manchester, recognizing the Concord Bhutanese community and the cultural significance of the event. The Mayor thanked the City Clerk, staff, ward moderators, and election volunteers for administering the election, noting that more than 1,000 residents registered to vote on Election Day commending the City's election process.

City Manager Aspell recognized the 10th anniversary of the Main Street reconstruction project and thanked those involved in its original planning and continued maintenance, particularly Jeff Hoadley and Matt Walsh. He also thanked Bob Bonenfant for supporting the City's ability to benefit from the City Clerk's services.

Mayor Champlin additionally congratulated the City Manager on being named Concord Citizen of the Year and acknowledged the community recognition of his service.

Adjournment

Action: Councilor Fennessy moved to adjourn at 9:49 p.m. The motion was duly

seconded by Councilor Kurtz and passed with no dissenting votes.
